title: JSON basics
description: A two-lesson example course: what JSON is, and how to catch a type bug in an AI-written config file.
rules: When the learner writes JSON, ask them to read it back as data types (string, number, boolean, null, array, object) before you comment on it.

placement.intro: Find out whether the learner has written JSON by hand before. Ask at most two short questions.

json.title: Read and write JSON
json.tagline: From the six value types to fixing a real config file.
json.placementHints: Start at what-is-json for anyone new to JSON. Start at fix-the-config, skipping what-is-json, only if the learner already edits JSON files by hand and can name its value types.

sources.title: RFC 8259: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

beats.goal: The learner knows JSON is plain text that describes data.
beats.content: JSON is a text format for data. A JSON document is one value. A value is one of six types: an object (name/value pairs in curly braces), an array (an ordered list in square brackets), a string (in double quotes), a number, true or false, or null.
beats.question: Before we go on: which of these do you think is a string in JSON, 42 or "42"? Why?

beats.goal: The learner knows the rules that trip people up.
beats.content: JSON is stricter than JavaScript. Names in objects must be strings in double quotes. Single quotes are not allowed. A trailing comma after the last item is an error. There are no comments.
beats.question: Predict: is {"port": 8080,} valid JSON? What would a parser say?

checkpoint.question: In your own words: what is the difference between {"port": 8080} and {"port": "8080"}, and why might a program care?
checkpoint.rubric: A good answer says the first value is a number and the second is a string, and that a program reading the value may compare, add or validate it differently (for example, a server expecting a number may reject or mishandle a string). Exact wording does not matter.

branches.when: The answer identifies number versus string and gives any sensible reason a program might care.
branches.message: You can tell the types apart. Next, a config file an AI wrote, with one planted bug.

branches.when: The answer misses the number/string difference or gives no reason it matters.
branches.message: Let's go over the six value types once more before moving on.

beats.goal: The learner reads a JSON file by value types, not by eye.
beats.content: When you review JSON, read each value and name its type. Quoted means string, even if it looks like a number or a boolean. "true" is a string; true is a boolean.
beats.question: In {"debug": "false"}, what type is the value of debug, and what might a program do with it?

bug.explanation: port was the string "8080" instead of the number 8080. A server that expects a number can reject it, or treat it as text.
bug.hint: Read every value aloud with its type. One of them is not the type the server expects for a network port.

checkpoint.question: Add a timeout setting of 30 seconds as a number, in config.json, then send the file and explain the type you chose.
checkpoint.rubric: The checks decide whether the file is right. For the explanation, a good answer says timeout is a number because the program does arithmetic or comparisons with it.

checks.message: config.json needs a top-level "timeout" whose value is the number 30 (not a string).

branches.when: The checks passed and the learner explains why timeout is a number.
branches.message: That's the path done. Your record has every step, and it's yours to keep.

branches.when: The checks passed but the explanation of the type is missing or wrong.
branches.message: The file is right; let's make sure the reason is clear too.
